newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt calls for halt to Jerusalem settlement.
newsitem.headline: Egypt calls for halt to Jerusalem settlement.

text.p: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak on Saturday predicted incessant violence until Israel stops building settlements in Arab East Jerusalem.

Mubarak, speaking to an economic conference of the ruling National Democratic Party, also said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu must abandon what he called a patronising attitude towards his Arab neighbours.
"Acts of violence and tension will not stop in the region unless building in East Jerusalem stops. There is no other solution," he told the closed-door meeting.
Information Minister Safwat el-Sherif, the government's spokesman, briefed government newspapers on Mubarak's remarks.

"President Mubarak said he had asked the Israeli prime minister to address Arab society in its own language...and to respect its culture. (He said) patronising language is unacceptable and no Arab will accept it," Sherif said.
"The solution is for Israel to find a way out, stopping building in East Jerusalem so that the region can escape from the crisis," he added, paraphrasing the president.
Mubarak dismissed a Netanyahu proposal to speed up talks on "final status" questions such as Jerusalem, bypassing interim Israeli withdrawals from parts of the West Bank.
"It would be hard to achieve and would lead to a vicious circle which sensible people could not accept," he said.

Mubarak did not mention any measures the Egyptian government was planning against Israel but he said that other states were frightened to continue normalising relations with the Jewish state and business people had started to stop dealing with Israelis.

In an interview with Israel's Channel Two, broadcast earlier on Saturday, Mubarak said that Israel needed to "get real" if it wanted peace in the region and that the only way to end violence was to address the reasons behind it.
He said Netanyahu, by not implementing peace deals signed with the Palestinians, had made the region unstable.

"I can assure you that (Palestinian leader Yasser) Arafat doesn't dare to give these terrorist groups an order to blow something up. No one has the power to control terrorism," he said, referring to the Tel Aviv suicide bombing last week.
The militant Islamist group Hamas claimed responsibility for the bombing, which killed three Israelis.
Israel has accused Arafat of giving a tacit "green light" for militant attacks. The PLO denies the charge.
"You (Israel) have to look for the reasons rather than who did it. You have to find solutions so that the people can live in safety and peace," he added.
"Let's play another game, let's get real if we want peace," Mubarak said.

Israeli-PLO talks have been in crisis since Netanyahu broke ground last week on a Jewish settlement in disputed Arab East Jerusalem. This has sparked 10 days of non-stop violence in Palestinian self-rule West Bank.
On Saturday, a Palestinian became the first fatality of the clashes after he was shot in the back by Israeli troops in the West Bank.

Egypt, which considers itself the unofficial sponsor of the peace talks, held crisis talks last week on the settlement and Arab leaders have since condemned the project in an Islamic conference in Islamabad and a meeting of the Jerusalem Committee in Rabat.

Many countries say the 6,500-house settlement violates an understanding that no one should take any action to change the demographic or geographic composition of Jersualem before its final status is negotiated.

But Netanyahu, who was elected on a platform that refuses to hand over occupied Arab lands for peace as stipulated by a 1991 Madrid peace treaty, has said the project was just a way to solve the housing problem in Jerusalem.

Mubarak told the interviewers that Israel was responsible for the violence and unrest because of its lack of commitment and that it could easily solve the thorny issue of Jerusalem if it implemented other peace pledges.
Egypt in 1979 became the first Arab country to make peace with Israel but official relations remain cool.

Mubarak, who took over after president Anwar Sadat was assassinated in 1981, has yet to visit the Jewish state and he told the interviewer he would only do so after "the agreements are respected and justice is done".
